set_d.passage:
The Bharatiya Janata Party-led government’s relentless zeal in over-regulating civil society organisations is on display again in the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, which it had sought to push through Parliament. After strong protests, it has now been referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC). In 2020, the government got amendments to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, or FCRA, passed that barred a registered body from passing funds to another, even one registered under the same Act, and cut the share of foreign funds that could be spent on administration from half to a fifth, among other restrictions. It now proposes to go further still by taking over the assets that the money built, even on the mere lapse of a certificate. Under the Bill, a donee organisation can lose its registration not only when the government cancels it, but when renewal is refused, not applied for, or not granted before the old certificate runs out. As soon as this happens, the organisation’s foreign funds and what was built with them will pass to a government-designated authority automatically. The property returns only if the organisation re-registers within a period the government has yet to specify, failing which it is lost for good. According to the Bill, a building put up only partly with foreign money will be taken over in full. The organisation must then apply to get back the share not paid for with foreign money. The Bill does allow for an appeal to a district judge, but only against what the authority does with the property later. The refusal to renew cannot be appealed against, and the organisation will not be entitled to be heard before the refusal is made. In essence, because the authority acts on the Centre’s instructions, the Centre can use opaque reasons to withdraw a licence, take over the property, and then direct the body now holding it.
It is not surprising that minority religious institutions have been the most alarmed. This is true of Christian organisations, which run thousands of schools, colleges and hospitals built and sustained with money from churches and congregations abroad. Hundreds marched in Aizawl, Mizoram, under a newly formed council of churches; organisations in Kerala have objected to the Bill; Nagaland’s Chief Minister wrote to the Home Minister seeking a parliamentary review; and the Tamil Nadu Assembly has also unanimously resolved that the Centre should withdraw the Bill. The Home Minister has assured church leaders that the Bill will not apply retrospectively, but the text of his own Bill says otherwise. A hospital built decades ago can still be taken over today because a certificate has been allowed to lapse. The JPC, to which the Bill has been sent, should redraft it to provide organisations with an opportunity to be heard before renewal is refused, as well as a right to appeal against such a refusal, among other changes that would make the regulation fair and transparent.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?

options.text: An overview of how minority religious institutions in India manage foreign funds and run public service establishments.
A critique of the proposed FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026, highlighting its harsh provisions, potential for executive overreach, and the need for structural redrafting.
A comparative legislative analysis of the 2020 FCRA amendments against the Joint Parliamentary Committee's recommendations in 2026.
An account of state assemblies uniting to challenge the constitutional authority of the central government regarding foreign contribution laws.

questions.explanation: The passage primarily discusses the stringent and arbitrary measures proposed in the FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026—such as property takeover upon certificate lapse and lack of appeal—while highlighting protests and emphasizing that the JPC must redraft it to ensure fairness and transparency.

questions.question: Based on the passage, what can be logically inferred regarding the Home Minister's assurance to church leaders?

options.text: The assurance aligns with the text of the Bill, ensuring that properties built before 2026 remain protected from takeover.
The assurance is contradicted by the text of the Bill, which allows long-standing assets like older hospitals to be seized if a registration certificate lapses today.
The assurance was formally accepted by the Tamil Nadu Assembly after reviewing the legislative clauses.
The assurance guarantees that district judges can strike down retrospective property seizures.

questions.explanation: The text explicitly states: 'The Home Minister has assured church leaders that the Bill will not apply retrospectively, but the text of his own Bill says otherwise. A hospital built decades ago can still be taken over today because a certificate has been allowed to lapse.' This logically supports the inference that the written terms contradict the verbal assurance.

questions.question: According to the passage, what specific restriction was introduced by the 2020 amendments to the FCRA?

options.text: It completely prohibited non-governmental organisations from receiving foreign donations from overseas congregations.
It mandated that all foreign-funded property be automatically transferred to state authorities upon certificate renewal.
It reduced the proportion of foreign funds that could be spent on administrative costs from fifty percent to twenty percent.
It allowed registered bodies to transfer funds only to organizations operating in the same state.

questions.explanation: The text directly states that the 2020 amendments 'cut the share of foreign funds that could be spent on administration from half to a fifth', which equals a reduction from 50% to 20%.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the author's tone toward the proposed FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026?

options.text: Approving and optimistic about state oversight.
Critical and apprehensive regarding government overreach.
Neutral and purely descriptive of legal proceedings.
Dismissive of the concerns raised by civil society groups.

questions.explanation: The author uses expressions like 'relentless zeal in over-regulating', 'opaque reasons', and stresses the need for changes to make regulation 'fair and transparent', demonstrating a critical and apprehensive stance toward the proposed legislation.

questions.question: In the context of the passage, what does the word 'opaque' mean in the phrase 'the Centre can use opaque reasons to withdraw a licence'?

options.text: Lacking transparency or clear explanation; ambiguous.
Scientifically precise and non-negotiable.
Unanimously approved by parliamentary consensus.
Strictly bounded by constitutional mandates.

questions.explanation: In this context, 'opaque' refers to reasons that are obscure, non-transparent, or hidden from public/legal scrutiny, allowing the government to act without clear accountability.

questions.question: What is the primary argument the author presents regarding the procedural unfairness of the proposed Bill?

options.text: It limits administrative spending so severely that organisations cannot hire legal counsel.
It denies organisations a hearing prior to renewal refusal and provides no right to appeal against the refusal itself.
It requires all district judges to report directly to the Joint Parliamentary Committee.
It forces civil society groups to re-register every month under state-designated authorities.

questions.explanation: The author highlights that 'The refusal to renew cannot be appealed against, and the organisation will not be entitled to be heard before the refusal is made,' using this lack of due process to demonstrate the Bill's unfairness.

questions.question: Suppose an organisation constructed a community centre funded 40% by foreign donations and 60% by local donations. If its FCRA renewal is not granted before the certificate expires, what is the direct logical outcome under the proposed Bill?

options.text: The designated authority takes over 40% of the property, leaving 60% under the organisation's immediate control.
The entire building passes automatically to a government-designated authority, requiring the organisation to apply to retrieve the 60% locally funded share.
The entire property is frozen by a district judge until the JPC evaluates the building's utility.
The local share of 60% is automatically refunded to local donors by the Centre.

questions.explanation: The text specifies that 'a building put up only partly with foreign money will be taken over in full. The organisation must then apply to get back the share not paid for with foreign money.' This applies as soon as a certificate runs out/lapses.

questions.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage regarding a 'lapsed certificate' under the proposed 2026 Bill?

options.text: A lapsed certificate triggers asset takeover only if the government explicitly proves financial fraud.
Passive expiration or delay in granting renewal carries asset forfeiture consequences equivalent to active government cancellation.
Organisations with lapsed certificates are granted an automatic five-year grace period to re-register.
Lapsing of a certificate only affects foreign cash reserves, leaving physical assets intact.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly notes that an organisation can lose its registration and have its assets automatically pass to a government authority not only upon active cancellation, but when renewal is refused, not applied for, or not granted before the old certificate runs out. Thus, passive expiration/delay has the same severe outcome as cancellation.
